parts.description: A clear glass pitcher with a flared rim, pouring spout, thick rounded base, and curved transparent handle.
parts.reasoning: The object appears to be an empty household glass pitcher with a thin-walled tapered body, thicker glass base, raised rim, spout, and a hollow loop handle. A realistic size estimate is about 0.22-0.26 m tall, 0.13-0.16 m body diameter, and roughly 0.18-0.21 m total width including the handle. Soda-lime glass density is approximately 2400-2600 kg/m^3, so 2500 kg/m^3 is used for the material density. Because the pitcher is hollow, the total mass should be assigned explicitly rather than computed from a filled convex collision volume; a typical empty 1-1.5 L glass pitcher with a thick base is about 0.9-1.3 kg, so 1.1 kg is a reasonable estimate. The center of mass is lower than the geometric midpoint because of the thick base and slightly offset toward the handle. Glass-on-common-hard-surface friction is moderate-low, so static friction is estimated at 0.35 and dynamic friction at 0.25; contact with rubber grippers will be governed by the combined material mode and will be higher. Restitution is set to 0.60, consistent with hard glass, though a lower effective restitution may be preferable if breakage is not modeled and excessive bounce is undesirable. For collision, a single convex hull would incorrectly fill the open mouth, spout region, and handle opening, while a bounding primitive would be much too coarse. A convex decomposition compound collider is the best default dynamic-rigid choice: separate hulls should approximate the main body, thick base, rim/spout, and handle segments. SDF mesh collision can be considered only if accurate inner cavity or handle-hole contact is essential and the performance cost is acceptable. A contact offset around 3 mm is appropriate for meter-scale units and thin glass features; a 0 m rest offset keeps the visible glass aligned with contacts. CCD is recommended because the walls and handle are thin and could tunnel through grippers or surfaces during fast motion. Compliant contacts should normally be disabled for a non-deformable glass object; if numerical chatter occurs, use very stiff, highly damped compliance only as a stabilization aid. Suggested velocity limits and sleep settings are conservative for manipulation and drop tests: max linear velocity about 10 m/s, max angular velocity about 60 rad/s, max depenetration velocity about 2 m/s, sleep threshold about 0.005, and stabilization threshold about 0.001.
